articles.title: Biodiversity emerges as a leading driver of urban green space management across Europe - Bioengineer.org
articles.summary: Biodiversity emerges as a leading driver of urban green space management across Europe  Bioengineer.org
articles.full_text:
A sweeping survey of European municipalities has found that biodiversity is no longer an afterthought in urban green space planning — it is now a central motivation for the people who design and manage the parks, lawns and green corridors of Europe’s cities. Researchers questioned 574 municipalities across 18 European countries and discovered that 85 percent of them consider biodiversity a key motivation in how they plan and manage public green spaces. The findings, published in the journal Nature Cities, offer one of the first broad, expert-based pictures of how Europe’s city administrations view the ecological condition of their own urban nature, and what they are doing to make it better.
The scale of the survey is notable. Responses came from countries as diverse as Germany, France, Denmark, Slovenia, Latvia and Luxembourg, with 612 individual responses collected between April 2023 and May 2024. Each questionnaire targeted the individual responsible for fundamental decisions about public green space in their municipality — from small towns of a few hundred residents to metropolises like Berlin, Paris and Vienna. The survey was translated into national languages to avoid misunderstandings, and participation was voluntary. The geographic spread spanned northern, southern, eastern and western Europe, although the authors acknowledge that voluntary participation left some gaps in representation.
The headline numbers are striking. Beyond the 85 percent of municipalities naming biodiversity as a key motivation, 82 percent reported providing training on biodiversity-friendly management to city administrators and staff. Three quarters said they take active steps to increase public acceptance of biodiversity-promoting management — a recognition that ecologically valuable practices, such as leaving leaf litter or letting vegetation grow wilder, can look untidy to residents accustomed to manicured lawns. Slightly more than half, 54 percent, involve their populations directly in green space planning and design, potentially seeding bottom-up initiatives for urban nature.
Yet biodiversity is far from the only goal. When respondents rated the importance of 13 goals for green space planning and management, the four highest-ranked were all related to the well-being of urban citizens. Promoting biodiversity ranked fifth, rated rather or very important by 83 percent of respondents. Twelve of the 13 goals were rated important by more than half of respondents; the lone exception was creating opportunities for urban gardening — the growing of fruits and vegetables in cities — which only 38 percent considered rather or very important, while 34 percent rated it as rather not or not at all important. The authors see in these results a clear demand for multifunctional green space, but also a risk of conflict between goals such as visual appearance, recreation and ecological value.
The survey also probed how municipalities perceive the ecological state of their own urban nature. Over half — 57 percent — rated the current state as good or very good, while only 11 percent considered it poor or very poor. A large majority, 68 percent, perceived improvement over the past decade, although about one in five — 19 percent — reported deterioration, which the researchers suggest could reflect ongoing losses in the quantity or quality of green space driven by urban development and increasing impervious cover. These are expert-based perceptions rather than detailed ecological measurements, but they offer a coarse and, until now, largely unavailable assessment of where European urban nature stands.
Statistical analysis revealed intriguing links between municipal characteristics and biodiversity priorities. The likelihood that biodiversity was considered a basic motivation increased significantly with the proportion of impervious, sealed surface in a municipality, and with a higher national quality-of-life index. The authors suggest a rationale: highly sealed municipalities often have limited green space, and expanding it through de-sealing is difficult, so improving the ecological quality of what already exists may be the most feasible strategy. The association with quality of life may reflect a shift toward post-materialist values, in which administrations can look beyond basic human needs and embrace the idea of multispecies coexistence in cities.
Other patterns followed similar fault lines. Training opportunities were more likely in municipalities with higher impervious cover, more northern locations and higher national quality-of-life indices. Citizen involvement in planning increased with both quality of life and population size, while actions to boost public acceptance rose with impervious cover and larger populations. The authors point to structural inequalities: wealthier, larger municipalities may have the financial and institutional resources for participatory processes and benefit from denser networks of universities, while those in countries with lower quality-of-life indices may be occupied with pressing challenges like housing, healthcare and transport, limiting their capacity to engage with biodiversity initiatives even when benefits are recognized.
Geography also colored perceptions. Municipalities further east were more likely to rate the current state of their urban nature as ecologically valuable, while those further south rated it less favorably — possibly because summer-dry southern cities, battered by heatwaves and water shortages, have green spaces that appear less lush and attractive. Perceived improvement over the past decade was higher in countries with lower quality-of-life indices. The authors stress that such regional and cultural differences matter for policy: frameworks aiming to support biodiversity-promoting management must be locally adaptable rather than uniform, a point reinforced by the finding that sealed, densely built municipalities are already those most committed to ecological improvement.
The study arrives at a politically significant moment. Current European Union indicators under the Nature Restoration Regulation focus primarily on the quantity of urban green space, whereas this survey offers insight into its ecological quality — the diversity of species and habitats that green space actually supports. The authors see encouraging momentum, suggesting that the positive trends they document might strengthen as European policy frameworks place growing emphasis on urban ecosystems, and they hope their results will inform targeted communication and locally adjustable strategies for municipalities.
Important caveats remain. Responses were collected from a single representative per municipality, which may not capture the full range of perspectives within local administrations, though the large number of municipalities mitigates this. Impervious cover was calculated from built-up surface within administrative unit boundaries that can include farmland or forest beyond the city center, potentially diluting the measure for some municipalities. The ecological assessments are expert judgments, not systematic habitat surveys, and more detailed evaluations of urban habitats will be needed to prioritize restoration. Still, the core message is clear: Europe’s municipalities overwhelmingly view biodiversity as a goal worth pursuing alongside — not instead of — the needs of their citizens, and balancing the two will define the next chapter of urban green space governance.

articles.summary: EU agrees to raise carbon market reserve cap to 700 mn allowances  Fibre2Fashion
articles.full_text:
Insights
- The European Commission has welcomed a provisional European Parliament-Council agreement to strengthen the Market Stability Reserve of the EU Emissions Trading System.
- The deal would let the reserve retain up to 700 million allowances, compared with invalidating holdings above 400 million under current rules.
- Formal adoption is still required before the amendment enters into force.
Under current rules, all emission allowances in the reserve above 400 million are invalidated. The agreed amendment would allow the reserve to retain up to 700 million allowances as a buffer to support future market stability and predictability, while preserving the system’s rules-based design and environmental integrity, the European Commission said.
The agreement follows the Commission’s April 2026 proposal, tabled after President von der Leyen’s announcement at the March European Council, and delivers on European Council conclusions issued on October 16. It also advances implementation of the One Europe, One Market roadmap agreed among EU institutions to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness by the end of 2027, according to the Commission.
First introduced in 2019, the MSR is designed to make the EU ETS more resilient by adjusting the supply of allowances in response to market developments. It reduces the supply of allowances to the market when there are too many in circulation and injects allowances when there is scarcity; it also contains price volatility by reducing auction volumes during periods of supply surplus and releasing allowances in periods of scarcity based on predefined rules, the Commission said.
The Commission said the agreement sends a signal that the EU is committed to a predictable and reliable carbon market, providing greater certainty for businesses and investments in clean transition. It described the deal as a first step towards wider modernisation of the MSR, for which further reforms were proposed as part of the separate MSR reform and the EU ETS review on July 17, 2026.
The European Parliament and the Council of the EU must still formally adopt the text. The amendment of the Market Stability Reserve Decision will enter into force upon publication in the Official Journal of the EU.

articles.title: The real test of India’s carbon market is getting the price right - Carbon Copy
articles.summary: The real test of India’s carbon market is getting the price right  Carbon Copy
articles.full_text:
In today’s geopolitical and trade landscape, a credible domestic carbon price is not just climate policy, but an industrial strategy as well
Visual Credits: Arkatapa Basu
India is putting a national price on industrial carbon for the first time. Under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), baselines and final targets have been notified for seven energy-intensive sectors covering roughly 490 industrial emitters. The world’s sixth largest economy is joining a global shift: emissions trading systems now cover about 28% of the world's emissions and have raised more than $100 billion a year through auction revenues and other forms of carbon pricing.
The debate so far was about whether India should have a carbon market. That is now settled. The harder one is whether the market India builds will actually work.
A new report from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) and Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), examines precisely that, drawing on the experiences from carbon markets in the EU, South Korea, China and the state of California in the US. The report’s central conclusion is that getting the price signal right in the early years will be critical in building confidence and credibility in the market over time.
One should start with why the price matters at all. The whole purpose of a carbon market is to incentivise emission reductions. International assessments estimate that a single tonne of carbon dioxide inflicts around $140-380 (₹13,000-₹36,000) of damage on society — through worse health, lower farm yields and harsher weather. An unregulated emitter pays none of it.
A carbon market exists to close that gap. If the price it produces is weak, the gap stays open, and the market becomes less effective.
India's carbon market design is deliberate. Rather than setting a single absolute ceiling on emissions, as Europe does, it has chosen an intensity-based system in which firms are judged on emissions per tonne of output, not against a national cap. That lets an economy growing at 6.6% to 6.8% a year keep expanding without the carbon limit constraining production levels.
Also Read: Can biochar be India’s missing link to carbon capture?
It is the right instrument for a country that still has to industrialise. Underpinning all of this, credits are issued only after a firm's performance is verified. While this design has much to commend it, it also raises a challenge that merits a wider conversation.
A fine balance
In an intensity-based market, economic growth can create both buyers and sellers of credits. Firms that outperform their emissions-intensity targets generate credits that they can sell, while firms that fall short must buy them. The balance between supply and demand therefore depends on how ambitious the targets are and which firms are expanding production.
Carbon scarcity does not emerge automatically; it is created through policy design. Set the benchmarks too generously, and the market fills with cheap credits that reward business-as-usual and send little signal to invest in cleaner technologies. Set them too tightly, and firms face costs they may not yet be able to absorb.
This is not a theoretical worry. Historical experience offers a useful lesson. Europe's carbon market, for example, struggled with low carbon prices in its initial phases, prompting a series of reforms to strengthen the market. It issued too many permits, prices fell close to zero, and for the better part of a decade, the market did little to cut emissions.
Asia has similar stories: in their early phases, carbon prices sat below $10 in South Korea and between $6-$8 in China, drifting up to only around $14 by late 2024 — numbers set more by administrative design than by real scarcity. The lesson is blunt: a carbon market is only as strong as the scarcity built into it.
There is a hard commercial reason to get this right, too. From 2026, the EU's carbon border tax will require importers of steel, aluminum and other goods to pay for the emissions embedded in them, in line with EU carbon prices. If India does not price its own industrial carbon credibly, that bill will simply be collected in Brussels. In today’s geopolitical and trade landscape, a credible domestic carbon price is not just climate policy, but an industrial strategy as well.
Learning curve
The good news is that India can choose not to repeat these mistakes. It also starts with a foundation: for more than a decade, the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme has familiarised energy-intensive industries with compliance obligations, third-party verification, and tradable certificates. While a carbon market is a different instrument, these experiences provide a valuable starting point.
Three priorities stand out.
The first is a predictable tightening path. A blast furnace or a cement kiln locks in emissions for 15 to 30 years. No firm will price carbon into a thirty-year decision unless it believes the targets will tighten steadily and will not be quietly relaxed the moment industry pushes back. Europe, having learned the hard way, now follows a predictable annual reduction in the number of emission allowances available to the market. The rate of decline increased from 1.7% to 2.2% from 2021 onwards, steadily tightening supply and strengthening the carbon price signal. Publishing a clear, long-term trajectory of this kind is the single most powerful signal the government can send.
Also Read: What can India’s bilateral carbon credit deals learn from the centralised global carbon market?
The second is a stability mechanism built in from the outset. Rather than responding to challenges after they arise, India can strengthen market confidence by embedding appropriate safeguards from the outset. Europe recovered only after it created an automatic rule that reduces the supply of tradable emission allowances when surpluses build up. A transparent, rule-based version should be built into the CCTS too.
The third is a thoughtful roadmap for sectoral expansion. Currently, the CCTS roughly covers 20% of India’s emissions. The immediate priority is not to maximize coverage overnight, but to make the initial design work well. At the same time, policymakers should start signaling how the market would expand over time to cover a larger share of the economy. Wider sectoral coverage can deepen the market, increase opportunities for cost-effective abatement, and strengthen the carbon price signal.
Also Read: India Has Potential to Build $45 Billion Biochar Carbon Removal Market by 2030: Report
Need for expansion
Market depth matters too. Today, participation is largely limited to obligated entities. In more mature carbon markets, financial institutions also participate, providing liquidity by matching buyers and sellers, helping firms manage price risk, and supporting more continuous trading. While limiting participation in the early years is understandable, greater clarity on whether and how market participation could broaden over time would help firms and investors plan ahead.
Both are sensible evolutionary steps rather than immediate requirements. The objective is not to make the market bigger for its own sake, but to provide a clear sense of direction for how the CCTS can mature as India's carbon market develops.
There is a quieter risk as well. India is running many climate and industrial policies at once, including renewable consumption obligations, efficiency mandates, production-linked incentives, the Green Hydrogen Mission, the Green Credit Programme and others. Each is valuable. But where they cut emissions in the very sectors the carbon market covers, they can drain demand for credits and depress the price, with no one intending it. The carbon market must sit at the centre of this architecture, with the rest calibrated to reinforce its signal, not undercut it. That calls for coordination across ministries, states and regulators.
None of these is a case for hesitation. It is the opposite. As IEEFA and EDF’s analysis makes clear, a well-built CCTS could become one of the most powerful tools India has to reach net zero by 2070 while keeping its industry competitive — steering capital toward the firms and technologies that pollute the least and turning a cost on carbon into an advantage for the cleanest.
But a market is only as good as the price it produces, and a price is only as good as the promise behind it. Europe learned that at great cost. Asia is still learning it. India, building with all of it in plain view, has the rare chance to get it right the first time.
Shuchi Malhotra is the Lead Advisor, Carbon Markets at the Environmental Defense Fund. Views expressed are personal.

articles.title: Biodiversity is a key motivation for European urban green space planning and management - Nature
articles.summary: Biodiversity is a key motivation for European urban green space planning and management  Nature
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Many urban green spaces are ecologically degraded. Yet, when designed and managed using ecologically motivated practices, green spaces can support biodiversity. However, many municipalities have not yet adopted strategies to enhance biodiversity. To better understand the importance assigned to biodiversity in public urban green spaces, we interviewed 574 municipalities across 18 European countries. Using a standardized questionnaire, we examined the underlying motivations, management goals and the measures municipalities used to support the public acceptance of biodiverse green spaces. Most municipalities (85%) reported biodiversity as a key motivation in green space planning and management. Many provided staff training (82%) and took action to increase public acceptance (75%) of biodiversity-promoting management. The reported perceptions of municipalities’ ecological condition were mostly positive, but 19% reported declines in the last decade. Differences between municipalities could be linked to regional and structural factors such as the sealed surface of the municipality, highlighting the need for locally adaptable policies for urban biodiversity.

Main
Increasing urbanization is a key driver of global biodiversity decline through habitat loss and fragmentation1. At the same time, urban green spaces such as parks, grasslands and forests2 have the potential to contribute substantially to the conservation of local and regional biodiversity3,4. In addition, urban green spaces can promote the well-being of urban residents5,6 and facilitate important human–nature interactions7. Research shows that the psychological benefits of urban green spaces increase with biodiversity, indicating that green spaces designed and managed according to ecological principles are more beneficial for both nature and human well-being8.
Policy initiatives such as the European Green Deal encourage cities to enhance the ecological quality of their urban green spaces9, which, on average, account for 40% of the land cover of European capitals10. However, many public green spaces are in an ecologically degraded state, often due to improper management or design11,12,13. Urban ecological restoration and biodiversity-friendly green space management are currently gaining traction among regional governments and city administrators14,15,16, as well as among urban residents17. Recent legislation, including the EU Nature Restoration Law, a continent-wide regulation aimed at restoring degraded ecosystems across Europe, has further underscored the need to improve the ecological quality of nature within cities18. Yet municipalities, the key actors in urban biodiversity management and planning, have rarely been the direct focus of research. It, therefore, remains unclear to what extent biodiversity is prioritized in municipalities’ urban green space planning and management across different countries and climates.
Effective design, planning and management of urban green spaces must incorporate human needs and perceptions as well as maintain ecological processes11. The success of biodiversity-friendly management of public urban green spaces not only depends on ecological expertise and commitment of city administrators16,19 but also on the engagement and support of residents20. Beyond implementing direct measures to increase the biodiversity of public urban green spaces, municipalities should also facilitate bottom-up, community-led initiatives to increase awareness and acceptance of biodiversity-promoting management, as well as encourage private action for urban biodiversity. Therefore, municipalities should support bottom-up initiatives that allow residents to express their preferences and actively participate in the planning and management of urban green spaces. Research has shown that citizen participation is one of the key success factors in the planning and management of urban green spaces, although outcomes vary according to geographical and regional characteristics21,22. However, it is currently unclear to what extent municipalities use such strategies to integrate biodiversity into public urban green spaces.
Despite the growing attention given to biodiversity in urban policy23, limited empirical evidence exists on how European city administrations prioritize ecological goals in the planning and management of public urban green spaces, and which measures they take to increase awareness and acceptance of biodiversity-promoting management11,15. The ecological quality of urban green spaces is shaped not only by local management decisions and actions but also by broader structural factors, including population size and density, sealed area and socioeconomic conditions24,25,26. Geographic context may further influence both ecological conditions and administrative priorities21,24,26. However, little is known about these drivers and how municipalities evaluate the ecological state of their urban nature over the past decade, limiting our understanding of whether we are on the right track to support urban biodiversity.
Europe represents a relevant case study due to its high degree of urbanization and the substantial heterogeneity among countries in both environmental and socio-institutional contexts. To address existing knowledge gaps, we assessed whether municipalities across Europe consider biodiversity as an important aspect of urban planning and management, and whether they implement measures to increase awareness and acceptance of biodiversity-promoting management. We further examined how municipalities perceive the current ecological state of their public urban nature and how it has changed over the last decade. In this study, we defined municipalities as cities or towns with its own local government, without imposing a minimum population size27. On the basis of urban ecological and socioecological theory, combined with expert knowledge, we designed a structured questionnaire to address the following questions:
Q1. Do municipalities consider biodiversity as an important aspect of public urban green space management and planning?
Q2. Do municipalities implement specific measures to increase awareness and acceptance of biodiversity-friendly management?
Q3. Which goals, such as promoting urban attractiveness, ensuring low costs or supporting biodiversity, do municipalities follow in their management of public urban green spaces?
Q4. How do municipalities perceive the current ecological state of their urban nature and its change over the past decade, and how is this correlated to the implemented measures?
For each of these research questions, we applied a two-step approach: (1) we provide summary statistics across municipalities, and (2) we assess how municipality characteristics (for example, population size, impervious cover, geographical location and quality of life) help to explain the observed differences.
Our study can provide valuable insights into the priorities of municipalities for the planning and management of public green spaces. The respective findings contribute to the development of targeted communication and policy strategies to address urban ecological degradation and to promote the biodiversity-oriented restoration of urban spaces.
Results
Survey coverage and respondent distribution
In total, 612 responses were received from 574 municipalities across 18 countries (Fig. 1). Most responses came from Germany (71), France (56) and Denmark (56), whereas least responses came from Lithuania (17), Finland (17) and Luxembourg (2) (Fig. 1). When adjusted for population size, the highest respondent-to-population ratios were observed in Latvia, Slovenia and Denmark, whereas Germany, France and Italy ranked among the lowest.
Motivation and measures for biodiversity
Most respondents (511; 85%) reported biodiversity as a key motivation in their green space planning and management. A large majority (425; 82%) provided training on biodiversity-friendly management to city administrators and staff. Slightly more than half of the respondents (299; 54%) involved their population in green space planning and design. Three quarters (397; 75%) reported taking action to increase the public acceptance of biodiversity-promoting urban green spaces (Fig. 2).
Goals for green space planning and management
Six out of the 13 goals for green space planning and management were rated as rather important or very important by more than 75% of respondents. The four highest-rated goals were related to the well-being of urban citizens (Fig. 3). “generally promoting biodiversity” ranked fifth overall and was considered rather or very important by 503 respondents (83%). Most goals (12 out of 13) were rated as rather or very important by more than half of the respondents. The only exception was “create opportunity for urban gardening,” defined as the practice of growing fruits and vegetables in urban areas, which was rated as rather or very important by 38% (230) and considered as rather not important or not at all important by 34% (206).
Perceptions of the ecological state of urban nature
Over half of the respondents (338; 57%) rated the current ecological state of their urban nature as good or very good, whereas 11% (65) considered it poor or very poor (Fig. 4a). A large majority (398; 68%) perceived an improvement in the condition of urban nature in the past decade (somewhat or considerably improved), although about one-fifth (111; 19%) perceived a deterioration (somewhat or seriously deteriorated) (Fig. 4b). Among respondents who rated the current ecological state as good, 76% (253) reported an improvement in ecological conditions over the past decade. This share was lower among those who selected neutral (113; 63%) and dropped to less than half among those who assessed the state as poor (44%, n = 27) (Fig. 4c). articles.summary: Envases taps Tata Steel Carbon Lite to cut packaging Scope 3 emissions  Packaging Insights
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways
- Envases is offering Tata Steel’s Carbon Lite steel to help packaging customers reduce the CO2 footprint associated with steel packaging.
- Tata Steel says verified emissions reductions allocated through the mass balance system can cut the steel’s associated CO2 emission intensity by up to 85%.
- The partnership targets Scope 3 emissions by linking packaging customers with upstream steel decarbonization projects.
Tata Steel Netherlands has equipped Envases, a global metal packaging manufacturer, with its reduced Carbon Lite steel offering for packaging.
While Tata Steel’s Carbon Lite is not a new steel grade, it now includes a mass-balanced offering that is said to enable brands to lower the CO2 footprint associated with steel packaging.
“With Carbon Lite, the CO2 emission intensity of the steel associated with the packaging can be reduced by a maximum of 85%. For fillers and brands that pack a lot in steel cans, the impact can be substantial,” Marnix Böggemann, marketing manager for Packaging at Tata Steel, tells Packaging Insights.
However, he adds that carbon reductions largely depend on the share of steel in individual company processes and products.
Through the collaboration, Envases and Tata Steel aim to provide a “practical and credible” pathway for companies to reduce Scope 3 GHG emissions — the indirect emissions that occur across a company’s value chain.
Mass balance accounting
Mass balance accounting is one method to track the amount of CO2 emissions associated with packaging. Companies record how much CO2 goes into the overall production system and assign that amount to certain finished products.
“Under the mass-balance approach, verified emissions reductions are allocated to specific steel volumes through a certified accounting framework, while the physical material characteristics [of the steel] remain unchanged,” says Envases.
The packaging industry is also increasingly using the approach in recycled plastic content assessments. However, environmental groups have warned that it could lead to “unsubstantiated claims” of the amount of recycled content in packaging products.
Last month, Dow and Amcor partnered on the Carbon Footprint Ledger (CFL) methodology to help packaging companies reduce Scope 3 GHG emissions. The CFL is based on existing industry mass balance approaches in GHG accounting.
Sustainable steelmaking
Tata Steel’s Green Steel Project aims to incorporate more sustainable steelmaking technologies at its site in IJmuiden, the Netherlands, to achieve net-zero steel production by 2045.
Böggemann explains: “The revenues from Carbon Lite sales are used by Tata Steel to accelerate further decarbonization projects, which in turn (once verified) enables us to offer more Carbon Lite steel.”
Last year, the Dutch government signed a non-binding agreement under which it would invest €2 billion (US$2.4 billion) in Tata Steel to improve the environmental sustainability of the steel giant’s IJmuiden facility by reducing CO2 emissions, reducing health risks, and addressing quality of life concerns for local residents.
Since then, Tata Steel has come under fire from the Dutch Public Prosecution Service, which alleges that the steelmaker allowed “undercooked coke to occur” at its facility. Coke is made by heating coal at very high temperatures with little or no oxygen, but if the process is unfinished, it can lead to higher releases of pollutants and gases.
Value chain collaboration
According to the companies, the partnership highlights the importance of close value chain collaboration “to progress GHG-emission reductions.”
“Through these collaborations, companies further down the packaging value chain can actively contribute to upstream supply chain decarbonization,” says Böggemann.
“By embracing an insetting approach, such as Carbon Lite, they can take meaningful responsibility for their Scope 3 emissions by supporting emission reductions where they occur within their own value chain.”
Steel is also the most recycled material in the world, says Envases, adding that it can be recycled without loss of quality. Earlier this year, Henkel introduced a low-carbon tinplate can packaging for adhesive solutions that offers a 62% reduction in CO2 emissions compared to conventional tin cans.

articles.title: Deoleo’s Manuel Ayuso on Sustainability, Responsible Sourcing and Olive Oil Value Chains - The CSR Universe
articles.summary: Deoleo’s Manuel Ayuso on Sustainability, Responsible Sourcing and Olive Oil Value Chains  The CSR Universe
articles.full_text:
The real test of corporate sustainability lies not in the commitments companies announce, but in the changes they deliver across the value chains that sustain their businesses. In agriculture, where environmental degradation, climate uncertainty and rural livelihoods are deeply interconnected, responsible growth demands a fundamental shift in how businesses engage with producers, manage resources and measure long term value. For India, where agricultural resilience and inclusive development remain central to the sustainability agenda, this raises a pertinent question: how can businesses make sustainability commercially viable while ensuring that its benefits extend to the communities and ecosystems behind production?
For Deoleo, the answer lies in embedding sustainability at the source and carrying it through every stage of the olive oil value chain. From equipping farmers with practical tools for more resilient agricultural practices to advancing circular packaging, cutting emissions and strengthening product traceability, the company is working to translate its sustainability ambitions into measurable outcomes. In this interview, Manuel Ayuso de Francisco, PMO & Sustainability Director at Deoleo, examines why meaningful progress depends on moving beyond compliance towards collaboration, accountability and continuous improvement, and how this approach can strengthen both business resilience and the wider ecosystem on which the industry depends.
Scroll down to read the full interview:
Q. How does Deoleo define responsible growth, and how do you see CSR and sustainability contributing to that vision beyond environmental compliance?
A. Deoleo defines responsible growth as creating long-term business value while generating positive environmental, social and governance outcomes across the olive oil ecosystem. Our sustainability strategy is anchored in our purpose, “caring for what cares for you”, and reflects our belief that sustainable progress strengthens the foundations of the business.
This approach spans sustainable agriculture, responsible sourcing, resource management, circular packaging, emissions reduction, traceability and consumer education. Through the Sustainability Protocol, we work with olive growers and mills to strengthen agricultural practices and resource efficiency, while working closely with our suppliers initiatives across packaging, waste and climate action extend these principles through the wider value chain.
Sustainability also helps build supply chain resilience, strengthen relationships with farmers and communities, respond to evolving consumer expectations and support long-term business continuity. When integrated into everyday decision-making, CSR and sustainability become important contributors to innovation, resilience and lasting value creation.
Q. The olive oil sector is closely connected to farmers, ecosystems and rural communities. What do you believe are the most important areas where companies can create shared value across this wider ecosystem?
A. Creating shared value starts at the source. The long term strength of the olive oil sector depends on the health of the land, the resilience of farmers and the strength of the communities around olive cultivation.
For companies, this means going beyond responsible purchasing and actively supporting better agricultural practices. Water and energy efficiency, soil health, biodiversity, emissions reduction and climate resilience are all areas where practical support can create value for producers and the wider environment.
At Deoleo, our Sustainability Protocol brings this approach directly to farmers and mills through training, measurement tools and support. In 2025, the Protocol covered 95 certified mills, more than 61,000 farmers and nearly 350,000 hectares of olive groves.
The opportunity extends across the entire value chain, from sourcing and production to packaging, distribution and consumption. When environmental progress, farmer resilience, product quality and consumer trust move together, sustainability becomes a source of shared value for the whole ecosystem.
Q. Deoleo’s Sustainability Protocol is central to its approach at the source. What has the company learned from implementing the protocol about making sustainability a practical part of agricultural production rather than simply a certification exercise?
A. One of our key learnings since introducing the Sustainability Protocol in 2018 is that sustainability has to work in the reality of agricultural production. Sustainability therefore becomes a driver of resilience, productivity and long-term farm viability, rather than an administrative requirement.
Q. How is Deoleo working to ensure that sustainability improvements at the agricultural level translate into stronger long-term resilience for the producers who form the foundation of the olive oil value chain?
A. Resilience starts with protecting the resources that farmers depend on. Water availability, soil health, biodiversity, energy use and changing climatic conditions are increasingly important considerations for olive cultivation.
Through the Sustainability Protocol, Deoleo provides farmers and mills with training, measurement tools and benchmarks covering areas such as water and energy management, emissions and sustainable agricultural practices.
We are also involved in the SOIL O-LIVE project under Horizon Europe, which focuses on soil health, biodiversity and climate resilience in olive groves. The objective is to strengthen the foundations of agricultural production so that land remains productive over the long term.
For us, resilience is therefore about building capabilities alongside environmental performance. When producers have the knowledge and tools to manage resources more effectively, the benefits extend beyond an individual farm. They support continuity of supply, consistent quality and the long term strength of the olive oil sector.
Ultimately, the protocol has shown us that achieving meaningful transformation in the olive sector requires a combination of clear standards, robust measurement and continuous training. Certification can validate progress, but education, collaboration and farmer empowerment are what make sustainability a reality on the ground.

In 2025, 40% of the plastic used in Deoleo’s bottles came from recycled materials, allowing us to reach our 2030 target five years ahead of schedule. We also reached 79% recyclable bottles, reduced plastic waste by 7.6% and gave a second life to 94.4% of waste generated at our factories through the Zero Waste initiative.
The next stage is about building on this momentum. This means increasing recycled content, reducing the amount of material used where possible and extending circular practices across our operations.

articles.full_text:
The United States’ National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has developed a revolutionary new battery that could power the country’s return to the moon while potentially also revolutionizing the way that we power electric vehicles here on Earth. The new technology can function at extremely cold temperatures, opening new possibilities for powering lunar rovers and tools, and could eventually make batteries for terrestrial applications safer, more versatile, and more efficient.
“The technology could eventually power lunar rovers, scientific instruments, and emergency equipment used by astronauts under NASA’s Artemis program,” states a recent report from Interesting Engineering. “However, the batteries remain small laboratory prototypes and have not yet been demonstrated in space,” the article goes on to note.
During thermal vacuum testing conducted as part of NASA’s Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS) project, the new ‘freeze-proof’ solid-state battery has successfully endured temperatures as low as 274 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 170 degrees Celsius). In addition to surviving these superlow temperatures without damage, the prototype batteries proved operational (although at a reduced performance level) in temperatures as low as 112 degrees Fahrenheit below zero minus 80 degrees Celsius), with more optimal levels of performance in the extremely impressive range of negative 76 to positive 176 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 60 to 80 degrees Celsius).
These findings are a big win for the SPEARS project, which is charged with developing batteries that can survive the extremely harsh lunar environment without a constant source of heat to keep them from freezing and thereby becoming damaged. On the South Pole of the moon, where the United States aims to go, temperatures can drop as low as 328 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 200 degrees Celsius).
Traditional lithium-ion battery models are no match for such harsh conditions. Typically, lithium-ion batteries pass lithium ions from electrode to electrode through liquid electrolytes. Solid-state batteries are therefore a far more promising technology for extreme cold, as they don’t carry the same risk of freezing in the cold and performing poorly in the heat.
Plus, the liquid electrolytes used in typical lithium-ion batteries are highly flammable and are becoming an increasingly serious fire hazard around the world. “Plain and simple, solid electrolytes provide a safer and more stable environment for lithium ions to move through, enabling faster charging,” Popular Mechanics wrote late last year in an article about emerging electric vehicle (EV) battery technologies.
While the EV industry doesn’t need batteries that can withstand temperatures in the hundreds of degrees below zero (at least not until Elon Musk colonizes Mars), NASA’s incredible breakthroughs in solid-state battery technologies could provide critical science and technology to the sector. The SPEARS project’s findings “could eventually translate into commercial terrestrial applications,” according to recent reporting from HotHardware. “Space-rated solid-state tech could very well enhance the safety, temperature tolerance, and efficiency of Earth-bound electronics, including EVs, commercial drones, cell phones, and grid-scale energy storage systems operating in extreme climates. For EVs specifically, this battery breakthrough could, in theory, lead to longer ranges in colder climates and/or during frigid winter months.”
Moreover, SPEARS is not the only project bringing together NASA’s astronautic aims with the country’s broader energy development goals. NASA has also partnered with the United States Department of Energy to develop next-generation nuclear energy technologies to power a new era of deep space exploration. “We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’ which represents a major transformation for space exploration,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said earlier this month. “Nuclear power will allow us to go farther, operate longer, and field more capable spacecraft and instruments than ever before. The work we’re doing today is laying the foundation for the fission-powered spacecraft of tomorrow and opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.”

From Geneva to Yerevan | International Geneva @ UN Biodiversity Conference
The 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference will take place in Yerevan, Armenia from 19 to 30 October 2026. This major event, convened under the theme “Taking Action for Nature” includes concurrent meetings of the governing bodies of the Convention and its Protocols: the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention (COP17), the twelfth meeting of the Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (CP-MOP12), and the sixth meeting of the Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits arising from their Utilization (NP-MOP6).
About the 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference
The 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference will take place in Yerevan, Armenia, from 19 to 30 October 2026. This major event, convened under the theme “Taking Action for Nature” included concurrent meetings of the governing bodies of the Convention and its Protocols, including the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention (COP17), the twelfth meeting of the Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (CP-MOP12), and the sixth meeting of the Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits arising from their Utilization (NP-MOP6).
The Government of Armenia will convene the High Level Segment of the UN Biodiversity Conference 2026 on 27 and 28 October 2026 to galvanize leadership and political momentum in support for the effective implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and other decisions expected to be adopted at the Conference.
The Leaders’ Summit on Biodiversity
The year 2026 provides a decisive moment to take stock of progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), renew political leadership, and accelerate action. Against this backdrop, the incoming Armenian Presidency of COP 17 and its concurrent meetings hosted a one-day, by invitation, Leaders’ Summit on Biodiversity, under the motto “Leaders’ for Nature” on 16 October 2026 in Yerevan, Armenia.
The Summit provided an opportunity to review progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, renew political leadership, and mobilize greater ambition and coordinated global action ahead of COP 17. It concluded with “Yerevan Declaration – Taking Action for Nature” reaffirming commitment to the implementation of the Framework, including the mission to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 and achieve the vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050. → Read more at:

State of Biodiversity Action Report on Progress in the Implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
The State of Biodiversity Action report on progress in the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, released on 15 October 2026, provides the first comprehensive global stocktake of progress towards the Framework’s 2030 targets and 2050 vision.
Drawing on national reports, updated biodiversity strategies, scientific assessments and diverse sources of knowledge, it assesses progress across all 23 targets, identifying achievements, implementation gaps and barriers. The final report brings together evidence from countries and stakeholders worldwide to examine where progress is advancing and where efforts must accelerate. It highlights the need for stronger implementation, coordinated action and increased ambition to translate global commitments into tangible outcomes for nature. As a key input to the Global Review at COP 17, the report provides an evidence base to guide decision-making and help Parties and stakeholders accelerate action to halt and reverse biodiversity loss.

In preparation for the 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference, various actors in Geneva, including the Geneva Environment Network and its partners, have organized multiple events.

As a global hub for biodiversity governance, there will be a strong multilateral Geneva presence at the UN Biodiversity Conference, providing contributions to the events and discussions. Additional organizations will be included as the Conference approaches.

The Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions will participate to underscore the role of the chemicals, pollution and waste cluster supports the biodiversity and health nexus to discuss how their work contributes to the work done under the CBD,

Biovision is committed to building sustainable food systems – from farm to fork. By supporting focused research and projects in sub-Saharan Africa and in Switzerland, we develop solutions for the future – through initiatives led by us or together with partner organizations.

Nature loss is a real business risk, yet businesses cannot halt nature loss on their own. Without strong policies and clear rules of the game, corporate action remains fragmented and limited in scale. Multilateral processes like the COP are essential to set ambition, align expectations, and create the pressure and accountability governments need to act, unlocking the conditions for business to invest, innovate and contribute meaningfully to protecting and restoring nature. Business participation at COP17 will be critical because: implementation is currently too slow, private sector action is essential, voluntary action isn’t enough and business voices shape ambition.

articles.title: Europe wants a circular economy. Will Africa inherit the waste? - The Africa Report
articles.summary: Europe wants a circular economy. Will Africa inherit the waste?  The Africa Report
articles.full_text:
A used laptop bought in Europe can enjoy a second life in Africa. But when that same laptop arrives with only a few months of useful life remaining, someone else eventually inherits the disposal cost. The same applies to ageing vehicles, electronic equipment and low-value recyclable materials that move across borders every day under the banner of reuse and recovery.
That contradiction sits at the heart of one of the most important sustainability debates of our time.
As Europe accelerates its transition to a circular economy, Africa must ask a difficult but necessary question: who ultimately carries the cost of circularity?
The European Union’s Waste Shipment Regulation (EU 2024/1157) seeks to strengthen controls on cross-border waste movements, improve traceability and ensure that exported waste is managed in an environmentally sound manner. Its ambition is commendable. No economy should outsource the environmental consequences of its consumption.
What happens in Africa?
Yet Africa’s experience teaches us that regulations should be judged not by their intentions, but by their outcomes.
For decades, used vehicles, electronics, plastics and other materials have entered African markets under the banner of reuse, repair and recycling. Many have expanded access to affordable products, supported small businesses and created economic opportunities. Others have left behind environmental liabilities.
A vehicle imported as affordable transportation may be approaching the end of its useful life. Electronics marketed as reusable may soon require disposal. Plastic waste exported for recycling may prove difficult or uneconomical to process. In such cases, economic benefits are captured upstream while environmental burdens remain with the receiving country.
That is not circularity. It is the transfer of environmental responsibility across borders.
A genuine circular economy cannot allow one region to close its material loop by opening another region’s waste challenge. Sustainability should be measured not only by what leaves a port, but by what happens after arrival. Are communities protected? Are materials managed safely? Does the receiving country gain lasting economic value?
Reject circularity without accountability
Africa should not approach this conversation from a position of weakness. Across the continent, repair, refurbishment and reuse have long been part of everyday economic life. From electronics markets in Lagos and Nairobi to repair workshops in Accra, Dakar and Johannesburg, entrepreneurs have extended product life and recovered value from materials others considered exhausted.
Long before circularity became a global policy priority, Africans were practising it.
A product likely to fail shortly after importation is future waste disguised as trade
Having worked across environmental compliance and sustainability in Africa and the Middle East, I have seen how regulatory ambition often collides with unequal implementation capacity. International frameworks frequently assume comparable enforcement systems, infrastructure and financing mechanisms. The reality is far more uneven.
This is why Africa must reject circularity without accountability.
The polluter-pays principle should not end when a shipment leaves a European port. Producers and exporters should contribute to inspection, traceability, verification and environmentally sound end-of-life management wherever their products ultimately arrive. Environmental responsibility must travel with the material.
The distinction between reusable products and waste must also be enforced more rigorously. A functioning product with years of useful life remaining is an asset. A product likely to fail shortly after importation is future waste disguised as trade.
Harmonised standards key
African governments should strengthen functionality testing, product standards and import controls while requiring greater transparency regarding the condition of imported goods. At the same time, the continent should continue building its own circular industries in recycling, refurbishment, remanufacturing and resource recovery.
A fragmented approach, however, will not be enough.
The African Union and regional economic communities should work towards harmonised standards for waste imports, inspections, customs classifications and digital traceability. Fragmented regulatory systems create loopholes that allow problematic materials to be redirected to jurisdictions with weaker oversight.
Partner, not repository
Africa should also advocate for stronger international cooperation to support monitoring systems, enforcement capacity and recycling infrastructure. This should not be viewed as aid. It is part of the shared responsibility required to govern global resource flows fairly.
Materials once considered waste are increasingly viewed as strategic resources
The broader debate is not really about waste. It is about economic power, industrial competitiveness and control over future resource value chains.
As the world transitions towards circular production systems, materials once considered waste are increasingly viewed as strategic resources. Critical minerals, batteries, electronic components and secondary raw materials will shape future industries just as oil and gas shaped previous generations.
The debate over waste shipments is, therefore, a debate about who captures value in the emerging global economy.
Africa must ensure it participates in this transition not as a repository for residual materials, but as a processor, innovator and industrial partner. Europe is right to strengthen its waste rules. But the success of circularity will not be measured only by cleaner cities in Europe. It will also be measured by whether African countries gain investment, technology, jobs and greater control over their resource future.
No nation should achieve sustainability by exporting unsustainability to another. If the circular economy is to become a cornerstone of the 21st-century economy, it must be built on shared prosperity as much as environmental efficiency. Otherwise, the promise of circularity risks becoming another chapter in a much older story: value flowing north while costs remain south.

articles.title: Due diligence in the paper & packaging sector: Five areas to watch - Freshfields
articles.summary: Due diligence in the paper & packaging sector: Five areas to watch  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
Oct 23 2026
Paper and packaging companies navigate a growing set of rules covering deforestation, forced labour, environmental claims, packaging waste and product design. These requirements increasingly reach beyond the compliance function into supply chains, product portfolios, customer relationships and transactions. For buyers, sellers and financial sponsors, the transactional implications are direct: a target with weak traceability or poorly documented compliance creates additional work and uncertainty, and affects how risk is allocated across warranties and indemnities. Regulatory readiness is becoming part of transaction readiness – a compliance gap does not necessarily stop a deal, but it can shape the work required to get it done and the price at which it is done.
A link to our EU and US regulatory map for the paper and packaging sector can be found at the end of this overview.
At a glance – five areas that deserve particular attention:
Traceability
Substantiating environmental claims
Changes to the economics of packaging
Allocation of responsibility across overlapping frameworks
Designing for future requirements
1. Traceability
Traceability is now central to operating in this sector. The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), the EU Forced Labour Regulation and the US Lacey Act differ in approach, but each raises the importance of knowing what is in the supply chain and where materials originate. For paper and packaging businesses, that means looking beyond the immediate supplier: where did the fibre come from, what other plant-based materials are used, and can supplier information be verified?
The question for any business is whether it has the information to understand its upstream supply chain, or whether there are still gaps. In a transaction, those gaps become the buyer’s problem. A target that cannot demonstrate traceability to the level that buyers now expect is a target with unquantified exposure, and that exposure tends to surface in diligence as warranty requests, price adjustments or conditions precedent rather than as a dealbreaker.
2. Substantiating environmental claims
Environmental claims are an area where a straightforward marketing statement can create a regulatory problem. Terms such as “eco-friendly,” “sustainable” and “carbon neutral” carry no single meaning; the regulatory question is what evidence supports the claim. In the EU, the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive restricts certain generic environmental claims and sustainability labels. In the US, the FTC’s Green Guides set expectations on claims such as recyclability and compostability, while state-level rules add a further, still-evolving layer.
A claim on a package or in marketing material needs to be clear about what it means, what evidence supports it, and which rules are in force (and enforceable) in the relevant market. For a business being sold, the position on claims matters in a different way: an unsupported or non-compliant claim is a contingent liability, and one that may not be visible without specific diligence on product packaging, marketing materials and customer-facing communications.
3. Changes to the economics of packaging
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is changing the economics of packaging. In the US, several states have introduced EPR schemes requiring producers to register, report and contribute financially to post-use systems. In the EU, the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) takes a broader, more harmonised approach. For many businesses this is a cost question as much as a regulatory one.
Companies operating across several jurisdictions need to understand the rules that apply today while tracking developments that could shift the position tomorrow. In a transaction context, EPR fees and compliance obligations feed directly into the operating cost base and into forward-looking assumptions about margins. A target that has under-provided for EPR costs, or that operates in jurisdictions where the fee structure is still being challenged in litigation, brings a layer of financial uncertainty that needs to be priced and allocated in the deal.
For energy-intensive paper and packaging businesses, subsidies and electricity-price compensation schemes are becoming increasingly relevant. In cross-border transactions, differences in national implementation of EU rules can create uncertainty. Due diligence should therefore assess the duration and scope of support measures, any conditions attached to them, and their accounting treatment, as these factors can directly affect the target’s cost base, earnings and valuation.
Strategic buyers may benefit from acquiring targets in jurisdictions where they already operate and understand the local energy and subsidy framework, giving them greater confidence in assessing future operating costs and assumptions.
4. Allocation of responsibility across overlapping frameworks
Obligations do not always sit neatly within one piece of legislation. The EUDR, the EU Forced Labour Regulation and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) address different risks and operate differently, but each can require businesses to understand aspects of their supply or value chains. An integrated approach has value here: supplier information, sourcing data, risk assessments and remediation processes may be relevant to more than one framework, and keeping them separate creates duplication and obscures the real gaps.
The CSDDD also illustrates why due diligence needs to be kept current — it was substantively amended in 2026, and the practical runway is longer than the transposition deadline suggests. But the transactional dimension is worth emphasising. In an acquisition, the question is not only what the target has done, but whether its compliance architecture is built in a way that can absorb the next regulatory layer. A target with fragmented, framework-by-framework processes is harder to diligence, slower to reassure a buyer and more likely to throw up gaps that have to be addressed between signing and closing. Sellers and financial sponsors who address these issues ahead of a process make diligence more efficient and strengthen their position in price negotiations.
These sustainability-related obligations sit alongside established environmental and operational risks, which remain central to diligence for paper mill and manufacturing-heavy targets. Buyers will continue to focus on site-specific permits, including their transferability and compliance history, particularly those relating to hazardous substances, wastewater treatment, energy infrastructure and legacy coal-related operations. Such matters can materially affect transaction execution and post-closing investment requirements.
5. Designing for future requirements
Regulation is increasingly shaping the packaging itself, not just how it is sourced, marketed or disposed of. The PPWR phases in requirements on recyclability, design and labelling over the coming years, and already restricts PFAS in food-contact packaging. The US picture is more fragmented, with several states restricting intentionally added PFAS in food packaging alongside evolving federal requirements.
For product and innovation teams, timing matters: packaging designed today may need to meet requirements that apply years from now, and retrofitting later is more difficult and costly than designing for the rules at the outset. In a transaction, this is an asset and capability question. A target whose packaging portfolio is already aligned with forthcoming requirements is more valuable, and less likely to need capital investment or product reformulation post-acquisition. The reverse is equally true: a portfolio that will need significant redesign to comply is a cost that has to be identified and factored into the deal economics.
In short
Due diligence in this sector is becoming a continuous exercise rather than an annual or pre-transaction one. It requires knowing where materials come from, substantiating environmental claims, understanding the cost implications of packaging waste rules, connecting compliance processes and building regulation into product design. It also requires comfort with uncertainty – some requirements are in force, others are coming, some are being challenged in court and others are still being developed.
For paper and packaging businesses in particular, this also means understanding the regulatory environment around energy costs, subsidies, electricity compensation schemes and permitting frameworks, as these can have a material impact on operating economics, valuation and transaction risk allocation.
The businesses that manage this well, and the transactions involving them, will be the ones where regulatory risk is understood early, allocated clearly and not left to surface in the middle of a deal.
